## 1. VS-Suite: Automated Consensus Virtual Screening Platform for Improved Screening of Small Molecules
- **2026-11-27** · bioinformatics
- why: Automated virtual screening platform integrating deep learning structure prediction and docking.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.17.766942
- abstract: Growing the recent advances in artificial intelligence and machine leaning (AI&ML) approaches accelerated small molecules screening against targeted proteins with limited computational resources and time. Finding accurate binding pose and affinity prediction is challenges task and traditional docking tools and lacks the reproducibility. Development of the Co-folding model is paradigm shift in drug discovery and development, allowing to predict protein ligand complexes without experimental crystal structures. Notably Boltz-2 predicts the complex structure along with binding affinity directly using protein FASTA sequence and ligand SMILES. Our previous studies confirmed that Boltz-2 is classify binder non-binders effectively. Autodock Vina and GNINA are widely used docking with knowledge and CNN based scoring functions allows to screen potential small molecules. We developed in-house VS-suite (Virtual Screening Suite) multi-environment conda orchestration designed to automate the docking workflow only using FASTA and SMILES string as inputs via streamlit-based browser GUI which integrates the boltz-2 for the complex structure prediction followed docking using AutoDock Vina for Gnina. Validation on 58 antiviral nucleoside analogues screened against SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro). VS-Suite is available at https://github.com/Vsubuchem-lab/Virtual-screening-suite-VS-Suite. This consensus approaches helpful in rapid screening of small molecules against selected targets. The findings and VS-suite support its utility as a rapid and reliable tool for hit identification and rational drug development.

## 2. FoXSight: Facilitating Computational Hit Identification in Crystallographic Fragment Screening Experiments
- **2026-11-24** · bioinformatics
- why: Computational method for hit identification in crystallographic fragment screening.
- topics: protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.01.763443
- abstract: X-ray crystallographic fragment screening reveals how small molecules bind to proteins, providing important starting points for drug design. Identifying these weak binding events remains difficult when electron density signals are noisy, partially occupied or obscured by solvent, and campaigns may comprise thousands of datasets. Here, we present FoXSight, a computational method for hit identification in crystallographic compound screening. FoXSight applies Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) filtering to multi-reference subtraction maps to detect recurring, target-specific density features associated with bound ligands. Its output maps remain visually interpretable and support subsequent ligand modeling. We evaluated FoXSight on in-house and public datasets spanning seven protein targets, comparing its maps with PanDDA where suitable comparison data were available. FoXSight was successfully used as the primary hit identification tool in a challenging crystallographic fragment screening campaign for human Cathepsin L, where the output of established methods was impractical to inspect systematically.

## 3. Target-specifc machine-learning scoring functions boost structure-based virtual screening for PfDHODH
- **2026-11-27** · bioinformatics
- why: Target-specific ML scoring functions for structure-based virtual screening of an antimalarial target.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.27.769741
- abstract: Plasmodium falciparum dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (PfDHODH) is a validated antimalarial target for which no inhibitor has yet been approved, and no target-specific machine learning scoring functions (ML SFs) have been reported for it. Here, we developed PfDHODH-specific ML SFs for structure-based virtual screening from a small dataset of 73 experimentally confirmed actives and 86 inactives, supplemented with property-matched (PM) and property-unmatched (PU) decoys. We compared five algorithms, several protein-ligand interaction featurisation schemes and classification and regression formulations under two evaluation designs: a Butina clustering split and a UMAP-based split in which each cluster of actives was held out in turn. The best model, a random forest regressor trained on PLEC fingerprints combined with Morgan fingerprints, was the strongest under both designs, reaching a normalised enrichment factor at 1% (NEF1%) of 0.617 on the Butina test set, compared with 0.323 for Smina, the best-performing generic SF, and an average NEF1% of 0.656 across the UMAP clusters (Smina: 0.362). Regression generally outperformed classification, and deep learning models were unstable with the limited training data. Adding PU decoys to the training set substantially improved enrichment for most held-out clusters, whereas the cluster most dissimilar to the training actives remained poorly predicted. These results show that target-specific ML SFs can be developed for a target with scarce bioactivity data, provided that algorithms, featurisation and evaluation design are tested comprehensively.

## 4. An AI agent guides a pipeline for selective protein interaction inhibitors from discovery across targets to preclinical evaluation
- **2026-11-24** · bioinformatics
- why: AI-guided pipeline for designing selective protein interaction inhibitors across multiple targets.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.23.768516
- abstract: A protein can engage multiple partners, making it challenging to disrupt disease-associated interactions while preserving others. We developed Bivexia, an AI agent that guides a multistage pipeline from discovery and de novo design through preclinical evaluation. Its decision rules are fixed in advance, and each prospective selection by the agent is cryptographically committed before testing. The objective is to discover small molecules that disrupt specified interactions of a target protein while preserving others. A compound advanced by Bivexia bound LAG-3 with nanomolar affinity and disrupted its interactions with tau and amyloid-{beta} while preserving binding to MHC class II and FGL1. It reduced tau and amyloid-{beta} burden in independent cohorts across two mouse models. The same rules gave three of nine hits on PrP and two of nine on LRP1, none in random controls. Our findings establish a framework for AI agents to pursue defined interaction selectivity across targets.

## 5. Multimodal Virtual Screening Identifies Candidate Inhibitors of Polyploid Giant Cancer Cells Across Breast Cancer Subtypes
- **2026-11-24** · cancer biology
- why: Multimodal ML framework for virtual screening to identify compounds targeting polyploid cancer cells.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.22.767421
- abstract: Polyploid giant cancer cells (PGCCs) are associated with treatment resistance and tumor recurrence yet identifying compounds that selectively suppress these cells remains challenging. Here, we developed a multimodal machine-learning framework to prioritize PGCC-suppressing compounds by integrating chemical fingerprints, drug-induced cellular morphology, transcriptomic perturbation profiles, and biologically informed molecular annotations. Using screening data from four breast cancer cell lines, we systematically evaluated feature selection, drug representations, and ensemble learning strategies. PGCC-guided feature selection reduced morphology dimensionality by 93.7% while identifying cell-cycle-enriched gene sets, linking predictive features to biologically relevant processes. An ensemble integrating complementary predictors achieved a mean Pearson correlation of 0.403 and an enrichment factor of 5.46 among the top 5% of ranked compounds. In held-out screening data, the ensemble recovered 27.9% of experimentally identified hits, representing approximately 5.6-fold and 2.5-fold improvements over random selection and the best individual predictor, respectively. We subsequently prioritized 21,367 compounds from an external library for experimental evaluation. Experimental testing identified six candidates that preferentially suppressed PGCCs in at least three paclitaxel-treated cell lines. Notably, AZD-8055 and voxtalisib reduced PGCC abundance by at least 70% across all four cell lines. These results establish a multimodal computational-experimental strategy for phenotype-directed drug discovery and provide new candidates for targeting treatment-induced PGCCs.

## 6. Dependence-Aware Conformal Prediction for 3D Uncertainty Quantification in Molecular Docking
- **2026-11-23** · bioinformatics
- why: Uncertainty quantification for molecular docking using conformal prediction and graph neural networks.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.20.768203
- abstract: Molecular docking plays a critical role in drug discovery by predicting three-dimensional (3D) binding poses of small molecules within proteins. However, docking predictions can contain substantial positional errors, making reliable uncertainty quantification essential. Conformal prediction (CP) provides a principled framework for uncertainty quantification, yet constructing compact 3D prediction regions with reliable joint coverage remains challenging due to heterogeneous atomic errors, dependence among spatial coordinates, and distribution shifts. We develop a dependence-aware CP framework for molecular docking that leverages a shared graph neural network (GNN) to estimate adaptive, asymmetric uncertainty intervals using local atomic and global molecular information. Copula-based joint calibration accounts for dependence among coordinate-wise nonconformity scores to construct compact 3D prediction boxes. We further introduce density ratio estimation (DRE) to adapt calibration under distribution shift. Experiments across three docking methods demonstrate that our approach reduces median prediction-box volumes by 37.40%, 95.00%, and 39.16% for AutoDock Vina, Protenix, and MedusaGraph, respectively, compared with a state-of-the-art CP baseline, while achieving empirical joint coverage close to the 90% target. Under the Molecular Group Split and controlled distribution shifts, DRE further reduces coverage deviations, highlighting the potential of dependence-aware and shift-adaptive calibration for reliable 3D molecular docking uncertainty quantification.

## 7. Resplitting LIT-PCBA with MolSCISSOR: A Memory-Efficient, Quasi-Deterministic Framework for Reducing Structural and Physicochemical Biases
- **2026-11-27** · bioinformatics
- why: Framework for reducing biases in virtual screening benchmark dataset splitting.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry, ultra large virtual screening
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.26.769502
- abstract: Reliable training-test partitioning is essential for developing and evaluating virtual screening (VS) methods, particularly in the era of machine learning (ML). However, existing molecular dataset splitting approaches do not simultaneously address key challenges in rigorous VS evaluation: cross-partition structural bias, test-set inter-class physicochemical bias, high memory requirements, limited scalability, stochastic allocation, a lack of automated optimization and of flexible training-test similarity control. We introduce MolSCISSOR, a lightweight, memory-efficient, quasi-deterministic framework for stratified data partitioning that integrates clustering and training-test allocation through multi-objective optimization. MolSCISSOR is used to repartition LIT-PCBA, a well-established VS benchmark comprising 15 target-specific datasets of experimentally confirmed actives and inactives, exhibiting substantial class imbalance, many of which are large-scale. We show that simple baseline ML models achieve significantly above-chance screening performance on the original AVE-derived partitions, indicating residual biases. The MolSCISSOR-generated benchmark, SPLIT-PCBA, is more challenging than both the AVE variant and that obtained using a BitBIRCH-Lean clustering-based workflow, with stricter cross-partition structural separation and improved physicochemical balance between test-set actives and inactives. MolSCISSOR mitigates stochastic variability, requires less memory than AVE, Lo-Hi and DataSAIL, and supports multiple split configurations with varying cross-partition similarity. MolSCISSOR and SPLIT-PCBA are freely available at https://github.com/caominhtr/molscissor and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23942580.

## 8. Structure-Guided Design of a c-Src-Inspired Polypeptide Inhibitor Targeting KRas4B-G12D
- **2026-11-27** · biophysics
- why: Computational design of a polypeptide inhibitor for KRas mutant using extensive simulations.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets, protein-ligand hit discovery
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.26.769561
- abstract: Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRas) is among the most frequently mutated oncogenes in human cancers, so that its direct inhibition remains a major therapeutic challenge. Here, we present a comprehensive computational investigation of a 41-residue chimeric polypeptide proposed as a potential binder of KRas4B-G12D. Our approach integrates conventional and enhanced sampling techniques, molecular docking, extensive molecular dynamics simulations, binding free-energy calculations, and per-residue energy decomposition analysis, amounting to a cumulative simulation time of 35.6 microseconds. Our work revealed that the primary state of the polypeptide (State A) consistently preferred KRas4B-G12D over the wild-type counterpart, irrespective of the nucleotide state. Structural and energetic analyses indicate that this selectivity of polypeptide arises mainly from interactions between its N-terminal region (residues 1-23) and the KRas switch regions, rather than direct contact with residue 12. These findings support an indirect ensemble-mediated recognition mechanism, in which mutation-induced shifts in the KRas conformational landscape modulate polypeptide binding. By revealing how a compact chimeric polypeptide can discriminate a single-residue oncogenic mutation through conformational recognition, this work establishes a benchmark for a new generation of mutant-selective peptide therapeutics, with the potential to transform the current strategies for the design of drugs targeting KRas mutations which are among the deadliest and least treatable in oncology.

## 9. Clustering conformations from molecular dynamics simulations by gradient flow segmentation of projected free energy landscapes
- **2026-11-27** · biophysics
- why: Presents a method to cluster MD conformations using free energy landscapes, aiding analysis of protein dynamics and ligand binding.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.25.769211
- abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations sample a continuum of conformations whose populations can reveal distinct protein structural states and substates as well as different ligand binding states. Determining which conformations belong to each state remains a central challenge in interpreting protein structural dynamics and ligand binding. Building on our framework for constructing free-energy surfaces from principal component projections of MD trajectories, we treat these surfaces as images. We adapt a method originally developed to segment cell nuclei in three-dimensional microscopy images and use the basin structure of the free-energy surface as the basis for clustering. We follow gradient flow toward free-energy minima and group neighboring regions by comparing the free energy along their shared boundaries with that within each region. When both regions contain resolved minima, we also test how far apart their cores are relative to their internal variation. Mapping the regions associated with the minima back to the original trajectories recovers the conformational ensemble in each state or substate and allows us to select a representative conformation directly from the simulation. We applied the method to conformational changes in the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and the leucine transporter LeuT, and to the binding conformations sampled by a small-molecule drug interacting with the PP2A scaffold PR65. By combining statistical mechanics with computer vision, this approach provides a structural interpretation of how sampled conformational populations are organized

## 10. Input Construction Accounts for Most PoseBusters Clash Failures on RNA-Ligand Complexes
- **2026-11-27** · bioinformatics
- why: Analyzes PoseBusters failures on RNA-ligand complexes, providing insights for docking and pose prediction validation.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, machine learning for comp chem
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.24.768943
- abstract: PoseBusters, a widely used test of the physical validity of ligand poses, was calibrated on protein-ligand crystal structures, and whether its checks transfer to RNA has not been measured. Applied without filtering the input to 2,970 deposited RNA-ligand poses, the receptor-clash check failed 527 of 2,931 (18.0%), and all but 7 of the failures were in covalently bonded nucleotides or in entries that contain protein, were solved by cryo-electron microscopy or were resolved at worse than 2.0 [A], so most failures are associated with which structures and ligand records entered the input set. On a high-resolution set constructed after these failures were attributed, the check failed 3 of 149 (2.01%; 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.00-4.58%) against 0.32% for the protein benchmark, a difference this set cannot resolve, and the PoseBusters calibration rule selected a threshold of 0.735 against the shipped 0.75. We give a seven-step dataset construction protocol and a tool, rnaprep, that implements its first four steps. On 139 redocking targets, with accuracy measured in the crystal frame without superposition, requiring a valid pose cost NucleoDock 25.2 points (69.06% to 43.88% within 2 [A]) and AutoDock Vina none, and cut the lead of NucleoDock from 38.9 points (95% CI 26.5-50.0) to 13.7 points, a lead not clearly distinguishable from zero (95% CI 1.3-27.5; cluster permutation P = 0.053). For these two programs in one redocking regime, the result supports reporting validity alongside RMSD in RNA docking benchmarks.

## 11. Predicted templates improve the prediction of antibody-antigen structures by AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2
- **2026-11-23** · bioinformatics
- why: Improves antibody-antigen structure prediction using templates from docking, relevant to computational antibody design.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.20.768078
- abstract: Motivation: In spite of the much improved protein structure prediction methods, the success rate remains low for antibody-antigen complexes. While this can be improved by computationally demanding massive sampling, results are still much poorer than for most other types of protein-protein interactions. In principle, improvement can be achieved by using templates that are close enough to the native structure of the complex, but these are generally not available for antibody-antigen complexes. Results: We explore the use of templates, generated by the computationally inexpensive rigid body docking program PIPER. Applied to a leakage-free antibody-antigen benchmark set, standard AlphaFold 3 with 1000 random seeds yields acceptable or better models as the top predictions for 56.2% of complexes. Adding the PIPER generated templates in the unmasked version of AlphaFold 3 either increases the success rate to 63.4%, or reaches the same 56.2% success rate in about 200 runs. The template-based approach similarly improves antibody-antigen prediction by Boltz-2. This result demonstrates that the space explored by the ML based approach can be expanded by adding templates prepared by traditional docking, compensating for the lack of evolutionary relationship and the limited availability of training data. Availability and Implementation: The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/login.php) containing the PIPER program is free for non-commercial applications and the program is available by request (https://www.vajdalab.org/). All other study data are included in the article and/or supporting information.

## 12. GlycanPUG: WURCS-Based Heterogeneous Graph Pretraining for Structurally Ambiguous Glycans
- **2026-11-24** · bioinformatics
- why: Introduces a graph pretraining model for glycans that handles structural ambiguity, advancing molecular representation learning.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.22.767969
- abstract: Background: Glycans orchestrate diverse biological processes, yet they remain underrepresented in computational biology compared to proteins and nucleic acids. Although WURCS 2.0 provides a machine-readable structural representation that preserves uncertainty, the evaluated IUPAC-based deterministic workflow processes 43.1% of the GlyCosmos-derived cohort examined here, motivating approaches that retain structural ambiguity. Methods: To overcome this limitation, GlycanPUG (Probabilistic Uncertainty-aware Graph) was introduced as a pretrained graph model for glycan representation learning. By leveraging WURCS 2.0, GlycanPUG represents candidate linkages and substituent attachments using weighted edges and uncertainty attributes within a heterogeneous graph framework. A 4-layer Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network with a dedicated node pre-enhancement module aggregates edge features weighted by the assigned edge weights, enabling representation of supported structurally ambiguous glycans without selecting a single resolved structure. The model is pretrained on a preprocessed subset of the GlyTouCan1 repository, which contained 253,596 entries before filtering. After excluding entries linked to downstream tasks and applying sequential structural filtering, 167,020 samples remained and were used for pretraining. Pretraining comprised nine self-supervised tasks. Results: Benchmarking on the GlycanML dataset demonstrates that GlycanPUG shows competitive performance relative to GlycanGT across multi-label taxonomy classification and binary immunogenicity prediction. Crucially, on datasets natively containing structural uncertainties (GlyCosmos, GlyConnect), GlycanPUG effectively processes additional structurally ambiguous entries, achieving 83.5% processable coverage across all glycans from all biological sources in GlyCosmos, with taxonomic classification performance (e.g., mean macro F1 of 0.7376 for Domain). Ablation of the node pre-enhancement module reduces macro F1, and post-hoc analysis identifies rank-dependent associations between structural uncertainty and prediction errors. All results reported above are averaged over ten independent random seeds (1-10). Conclusions: GlycanPUG broadens the set of glycans that can be represented while retaining supported structural ambiguities.

## 13. ViruDB: An Assay-Aware Molecular Database and Endpoint-Adaptive Multimodal Learning Framework for Antibiofilm, Quorum-Sensing Inhibition, and Antivirulence Research
- **2026-11-23** · microbiology
- why: Develops a multimodal learning framework for predicting antibiofilm and quorum-sensing inhibition activity using molecular representations.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.21.768264
- abstract: Antibiofilm and quorum-sensing inhibitory molecules have become increasingly attractive candidates to complement traditional antibacterial approaches, but the experimental evidence ranges from heterogeneous assays, organisms, methods of activity measurement, and chemical representation. We created ViruDB, a molecular evidence resource that is assay-aware, and tested an endpoint-adaptive multimodal learning framework for quantitative activity prediction. Curated collection of 8765 experimental evidence records for 3563 unique molecules: 2,959 quantitative observations, of which 2,345 were antibiofilm, 569 were quorum-sensing inhibition [QSI], and 45 were antivirulence. Molecular representations included 217 2D descriptors from RDKit, 2,048-bit ECFP4 fingerprints, molecular graphs, and some information about the biological context. A molecule- and scaffold-disjoint primary partition was used, which resulted in 2,339 observations in the training set, 265 observations in the validation set and 355 observations in the independent test set. ViruFusion-TaskExpert-MTL and an endpoint specific combination with classical regressors were selected by validation. The final predictor yielded an RMSE value of 0.5460 and an R2 of 0.4816 on the antibiofilm activity dataset (n=286) and an RMSE value of 0.5744 and an R2 of 0.4082 on the QSI dataset (n=67) in the reported frozen independent evaluation. Exploratory anti-virulence regression (n=2 test observations). The results validate quantitative, endpoint based prioritization under chemical novelty and highlight the significance of assay provenance, assay leakage control and external biological assay validation.

## 14. Discovery and Optimization of Indoline-2-Carboxamide-Based FBXO31 Recruiters for Targeted Protein Degradation
- **2026-11-24** · biochemistry
- why: Discovery and optimization of FBXO31 recruiters for targeted protein degradation, advancing PROTACs and emerging E3 ligases.
- topics: first in class / emerging targets, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.23.768409
- abstract: Expanding the repertoire of chemically recruitable E3 ligases is critical for advancing targeted protein degradation (TPD). FBXO31 has recently emerged as a promising E3 ligase for TPD, but existing peptide-derived recruiters exhibit limited degradation potency and efficacy at endogenous FBXO31 expression levels. Here, we report the discovery and optimization of indoline-2-carboxamide-based FBXO31 recruiters through structure-activity relationship studies. Optimization of the recruiter scaffold and linker yielded JZ26, a highly potent degrader that induced near-complete FKBP12 degradation at endogenous FBXO31 expression levels (DC50 = 2.5 nM, Dmax = 91%). JZ26 also induced potent FKBP12 degradation in primary mouse fibroblasts expressing FBXO31. Furthermore, the optimized recruiter was incorporated into bifunctional degraders targeting BRD9 and SMARCA2, demonstrating its applicability to multiple protein targets.

## 15. Development of a Novel Multitarget Directed Ligand (MTDL), LCI132 for the Polypharmaceutical Treatment of High-Risk MYCN Amplified Neuroblastoma
- **2026-11-24** · cancer biology
- why: Describes in silico design of a first-in-class multitarget ligand for MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma.
- topics: computational medicinal chemistry, first in class / emerging targets
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.22.768303
- abstract: MYCN-amplified neuroblastoma (MNA-NB) is associated with poor prognosis due to the development of resistance to current aggressive therapy and to the subsequent limited response to single agent targeted therapeutics in the relapse setting. Herein, we describe the in silico design and development of the first-in-class nanomolar potent, selective, multitarget directed ligand (MTDL) against PI3K, BRD4, CDK4/6/9 and Aurora kinases A/B, LCI132, for the polypharmaceutical treatment of MNA-NB. LCI132 demonstrates a favorable safety and pharmacokinetics profile, suppresses viability, induces apoptosis in MNA-NB and inhibits in vivo tumor growth with no toxicity. Mechanistically our data show that LCI132 orthogonally inhibits MYCN transcription and induces proteasome mediated MYCN degradation. We and others recently observed an augmented cytostatic effect of combining CDK4/6 inhibitors with retinoic acid in MNA-NB models and the associated disruption of core regulatory circuits. Importantly, this was not associated with the induction of apoptosis. The combined treatment of MNA-NB cells with retinoic acid and LCI132 synergistically inhibited cellular proliferation and induced apoptosis in MNA-NB cell lines and ex vivo patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models. Combination of LCI132 and ATRA treatment effectively reduces levels of MYCN and alters the expression of CRC transcription factors. Collectively, our study provides mechanistic insights and a rationale for the combined use of ATRA and a MTDL, LCI132 as a novel polypharmaceutical therapeutic strategy for the treatment of MNA-NB NB.

## 16. GlycoBind: a general toolkit for protein-glycan binding prediction
- **2026-11-26** · bioinformatics
- why: Presents a deep-learning toolkit for protein-glycan binding prediction, advancing ML and docking methods.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.25.769100
- abstract: Protein-glycan recognition controls immune responses, host-pathogen adhesion, cell signalling and the functional organization of the glycocalyx. Computational models can predict protein binding to monosaccharides or short oligosaccharides, but predicting binding to structurally diverse intact glycans remains challenging. Here we present GlycoBind, a general toolkit that accepts a protein structure in Protein Data Bank (PDB) format and an International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC)-condensed glycan, and returns a binding score without requiring a protein-glycan complex or a docking pose. GlycoBind adopts the frozen residue-state representation of DeepGlycanSite, a carbohydrate-binding-site predictor, and combines this protein representation with frozen GlycanGT graph representations through a compact trainable classifier. Across five protein-grouped holdouts, GlycoBind achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.767. On six external glycan-array datasets after exact protein and glycan cleaning for both models, GlycoBind showed higher aggregate binding-strength ranking performance and stronger recovery of high-intensity binding pairs than the existing models. By prioritizing high-intensity pairs for experimental follow-up, GlycoBind may support mechanistic studies of protein-glycan recognition and the rational development of glycan-targeted therapeutics.

## 17. Automated benchmarking with structured variant effect data
- **2026-11-27** · bioinformatics
- why: Introduces a standardized benchmarking framework for protein variant effect prediction, relevant to ML models.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.27.769673
- abstract: Protein variant effect prediction (VEP) has a wide range of applications, from describing the role of mutations in human disease to improving enzymes for industrial applications. VEP is now predominantly powered by machine learning models and high-throughput experimentation. Progress in this field depends on fair and systematic model comparison, which is complicated by the heterogeneity of VEP tasks and the diversity of model implementations. ProteinGym is the most widely used VEP benchmark, but it does not have a standard representation for datasets or models. This makes it difficult for others to run their own benchmarks with it and for the benchmark to keep up with new datasets and models. We address these shortcomings with the ProteinGym framework (PGF), which standardizes dataset representations, model interfaces, and evaluation protocols. The PGF consists of two packages: proteingym-base, which provides schemas for composing datasets and the PGDATA archive format, a standardized representation of VEP datasets, and proteingym-benchmark, which provides automated benchmarking of containerized models. As an example of a new experiment, we use the PGF to measure the ability of three supervised models to identify variants with property values that exceed those in the training set, a common objective in protein engineering. The PGF is available at https://github.com/ProteinGym.

## 18. AI-Driven Prediction of Drug-Target Interactions for New Chemical Entities
- **2026-11-27** · pharmacology and toxicology
- why: Presents AI-driven prediction of drug-target interactions using fingerprints and XGBoost, directly relevant to computational drug discovery.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.18.767501
- abstract: BackgroundModels that Ranking compounds may improve efficiency in drug discovery; however, due to similar chemistry in train/test sets, performance is often measured using random data splits. Here, we assess the predictive performance on completely novel compounds. MethodExact Ki values from BindingDB v202609 were used to create a dataset of 421,968 unique ligand-protein interactions. Interactions were defined as active if Ki [≤] 100 nM (53% active). Fingerprints (MACCS, ECFP4/ECFP6), six physicochemical properties, nine ADMET-AI predicted properties and amino acid composition of proteins were used as features, and interactions were classified with XGBoost. Thresholds were optimised on the validation set. External validation was performed using 1,524 target-compound pairs with no exact match in BindingDB. Compounds were defined as active if pChEMBL [≥] 6. ResultsUsing all three fingerprints, the best performance was achieved with ECFP6 (ROC-AUC 0.9125 [95%CI: 0.9105-0.9145], PR-AUC 0.9222, MCC 0.6613) on 84,394 hidden interactions. Performance dropped significantly on external validation with novel compounds. The lowest drop was seen with ECFP6, with ROC-AUC 0.8040 and MCC 0.4701. All three fingerprints showed a decrease in performance. Performance decreased significantly (by [~]0.11 ROC-AUC and [~]0.19 MCC) when applied to novel compounds compared to performance in random splits. Uncertainty in performance is much less ([~]{+/-}0.02). ConclusionGradient boosting using fingerprints retains some predictive performance in novel compounds. However, performance in random splits overestimates performance in external validation. This is due to several factors including chemical novelty, mismatch between classes and mismatch between ADMET features in train/validation sets. This is discussed

## 19. Distill-Mol: Learning unified molecular representations via cross-modal fusion and hierarchical geometric distillation
- **2026-11-28** · bioinformatics
- why: Proposes a multimodal molecular representation learning framework integrating SMILES, topology, and 3D geometry, advancing ML for molecular property prediction.
- topics: machine learning for comp chem, computational medicinal chemistry
- https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.11.17.767226
- abstract: Molecular representation learning aims to link molecular structures to downstream tasks in drug discovery and materials design. Molecules contain multi-level information, including semantic, topological, and geometric features. However, existing methods often rely on single-modality representations or shallow fusion strategies, limiting their ability to capture complex structure-property relationships. To address this issue, this paper proposes Distill-Mol, a multimodal molecular representation learning framework that formulates molecular representation learning as a language-structure-physics (LSP) collaborative modeling problem. Distill-Mol aligns SMILES semantics, molecular topology, and three-dimensional geometric information in a shared representation space and transfers geometric knowledge from a teacher trained with conformation angle noise to a student trained with coordinate Gaussian noise, enhancing geometric consistency and structural interpretability. In the fusion stage, cross-modal interaction and adaptive gating integrate complementary semantic, topological, and geometric information into task-adaptive molecular representations. Experimental results on MoleculeNet and QM9 demonstrate that Distill-Mol achieves competitive performance across diverse molecular prediction tasks. Additional experiments on DTA and DTI benchmarks further evaluate its applicability to biomedical interaction prediction. Ablation studies, perturbation validation, and interpretability analyses show that Distill-Mol learns task-relevant multimodal representations, improving predictive performance, robustness, and structural interpretability.
